abstract_text:
PROJECT SUMMARY
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a life-long neurodevelopmental condition that impacts ~1% of the global
population. Affecting ~90% of individuals with ASD, somatosensory dysfunction is a burdensome feature of ASD
pathophysiology that emerges early in development. Caregivers of ASD individuals often report challenges in
bonding through affective touch, observing preferences or aversions to specific textures, sensory seeking
behavior, and difficulty in filtering sensory information. All affects one’s ability to learn, socialize and participate
in everyday activities. The goal of this project is to define a novel mechanism by which haploinsufficiency of
SCN2A—the gene most strongly associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)—disrupts function at the cell,
circuit, and behavior level to alter sensory perception.
The gene SCN2A encodes the sodium channel NaV1.2, and is expressed throughout neocortical excitatory
neuron dendrites, whose function is critical for proper integration of synaptic inputs. How these dendritically
localized channels aid in neocortical function in vivo, and how circuits adapt to loss of dendritic excitability is
poorly understood.
In the mentored phase (K99), I will test the central hypothesis that Scn2a haploinsufficiency (Scn2a+/-) disrupts
dendritic integration in the somatosensory cortex, leading to impaired sensory perception, modeling a key cellular
mechanism of ASD-associated dysfunction. First, I will combine 2-photon calcium imaging of L5PN dendrites
with a behavioral paradigm to test whether Scn2a+/- mice exhibit a shifted perceptual threshold for passive
whisker stimulation. Second, I will use ex vivo acute slice preparations and in vivo 2-photon calcium imaging to
test how Scn2a+/- disrupts functional coupling between basal and apical dendritic compartments, thereby
impairing dendritic integration. The resulting data will link cellular dysfunction to impaired sensory behavior.
In the independent phase (R00) of this award will focus on determining how Scn2a haploinsufficiency disrupts
higher-order cortico-thalamo-cortical circuits that integrate contextual information to shape sensory perception.
I will test how Scn2a+/- disrupts posterior medial thalamus (POm)—a higher order thalamic somatosensory
nucleus—feedback at L5PN apical dendrites, POm intrinsic excitability, and whether Scn2a+/- disrupts functional
coupling between POm axons and L5PN dendrites in vivo. This work will establish a new framework for how
disrupted cortico-thalamo-cortical feedback loops cause sensory dysfunction in ASD.
Guided by my mentors, Dr. Kevin Bender (UCSF) and Dr. Daniel Feldman (UC Berkeley) and advisors Dr. Vijay
M K Namboodiri (UCSF) and Dr. Massimo Scanziani (UCSF/HHMI), I will acquire essential technical and
scientific expertise that will be crucial for setting the basis of my independent research program. Combined with
robust mentorship, collaboration and UCSF’s vibrant neuroscience community, this training will ensure my
successful transition to independence.
project_title: Examining Scn2a loss of function in sensory perception
phr_text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects approximately 1% of the
population, and is defined by social communication impairments, repetitive behaviors, and alterations in sensory
processing. This work will reveal how perturbations in the autism-linked gene SCN2A affect neocortical function
that shapes sensory perception. Resolving this critical knowledge gap will provide insight into how cortical and
subcortical sensory networks adapt—or fail to adapt—to SCN2A loss, providing new insight into mechanisms of
sensory dysfunction in ASD.
